prompt: Which port-security violation mode drops violating frames, logs them and keeps forwarding traffic from secure MACs?
options: shutdown
disabled
protect
restrict
explanation: Restrict drops violating frames, logs them and counts them, while the port stays up. Protect drops silently, and shutdown err-disables the port.

whyWrong.0: Shutdown err-disables the port and stops permitted traffic too.
whyWrong.1: Disabled is not a violation mode.
whyWrong.2: Protect drops frames but does not log or count them.

prompt: switchport port-security is entered on an access port with no other port-security commands. Which two settings apply? (Choose two.)
options: The maximum is one secure MAC
The aging interval is five minutes
Sticky learning is enabled
The violation mode is shutdown
The violation mode is restrict
explanation: The defaults are a maximum of 1 secure MAC address and violation mode shutdown. Sticky learning and aging are off.

whyWrong.1: Aging is 0 by default, which means disabled.
whyWrong.2: Sticky learning is off until you enable it.

prompt: Which two statements correctly describe DAI? (Choose two.)
options: DAI authenticates the user who owns a MAC address
Every inter-switch trunk must bypass ARP inspection
An explicit ARP ACL can permit a verified static host
DHCP snooping trust automatically makes an interface ARP trusted
DHCP bindings can validate a client's sender IP/MAC claim
explanation: DAI checks the ARP sender IP and MAC against the DHCP snooping bindings, and an ARP ACL can permit a static host with no binding. DAI trust is a separate setting from DHCP snooping trust.

whyWrong.0: Checking an IP/MAC pair does not authenticate a user.
whyWrong.1: Trunks are not automatically exempt from inspection.
whyWrong.3: DAI trust needs its own ip arp inspection trust.

prompt: Which optional DAI validation detects an Ethernet source MAC that differs from the ARP sender hardware address?
options: lease-time
dst-mac
src-mac
ip
explanation: src-mac compares the Ethernet source MAC with the ARP sender MAC. dst-mac checks the destination side and ip checks invalid IP values.

whyWrong.0: lease-time is not a DAI validation keyword.
whyWrong.1: dst-mac compares the Ethernet destination with the ARP target MAC in replies.
whyWrong.3: ip checks for invalid IP addresses in ARP fields.

prompt: A port has storm-control broadcast level set and no storm-control action. What happens when broadcasts reach the rising threshold?
options: Drop broadcasts on the port until they subside.
Send a notification without suppressing any traffic.
Change the port to an STP alternate role.
Err-disable the entire selected interface.
explanation: The default action is to drop the storm traffic until it falls below the falling threshold. Other traffic keeps flowing and the port stays up.

whyWrong.1: A notification needs a separate action setting.
whyWrong.2: Storm control does not change STP roles.
whyWrong.3: Err-disable needs storm-control action shutdown.

prompt: Why are many forged source MAC addresses a Layer 2 security problem?
options: They can force known unicast to flood across every VLAN regardless of policy.
They can authenticate forged senders by adding more entries to the MAC table.
They can make unknown destinations use only their last learned physical port.
They can pressure learning resources and increase unknown-unicast flooding.
explanation: Forged addresses fill the MAC address table. The switch then cannot learn real hosts and floods their traffic.

whyWrong.0: Known unicast is still forwarded normally and VLANs still separate traffic.
whyWrong.1: Learning a MAC does not authenticate anyone.
whyWrong.2: An unknown destination has no learned port to use.

prompt: What does an accepted secure source MAC show about the sender?
options: It proves the logged-in user owns the physical device.
It establishes that the IP and ARP claims are also authorized.
It proves the device’s application traffic is harmless.
It establishes that the source matches the configured MAC policy.
explanation: Port security checks only the source MAC against its policy. It does not authenticate a user or approve IP, ARP or application traffic.

whyWrong.0: A MAC can be spoofed, so it does not identify a user.
whyWrong.1: Other controls must check IP and ARP claims.
whyWrong.2: An allowed MAC says nothing about application safety.

exhibit.title: SW1: port-security status (excerpt)
exhibit.text:
Port Status             : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode          : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses   : 1
Total MAC Addresses     : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses    : 1
Security Violation Count: 1

prompt: PC-A is the authorized sticky device, and a different PC is plugged into Fa0/1. What restores the one-device policy?
options: Keep the new PC connected and raise the maximum to two
Reconnect PC-A, then shut and re-enable Fa0/1
Reconnect PC-A and wait for the default automatic recovery
Leave the new PC connected and clear all sticky entries
explanation: Secure-shutdown means the port was err-disabled by a violation. Reconnect PC-A, then shut and no shut Fa0/1.

whyWrong.0: Raising the maximum authorizes a second device.
whyWrong.2: Automatic recovery is off unless you enable it for this cause.
whyWrong.3: Clearing sticky entries lets the new device be learned.

exhibit.title: SW1 command result
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
Command rejected: FastEthernet0/1 is a dynamic port.

prompt: Fa0/1 connects one untagged PC and port security is rejected. What do you fix first?
options: Configure a native VLAN on the PC
Enable trunk negotiation on the PC
Enable port security globally
Set the port to static access mode
explanation: Port security needs a static access or trunk port, and this port is still dynamic. Enter switchport mode access, then enable port security.

whyWrong.0: A native VLAN does not fix the dynamic mode.
whyWrong.1: An ordinary PC does not negotiate a trunk.
whyWrong.2: Port security is enabled per interface, not globally.

prompt: A sticky address was learned after the last save and power was lost before another save. What do you expect after restart?
options: Startup configuration does not contain that new address
The switch restores it from its ordinary MAC table
The unsaved address becomes a permanent static entry
The address persists because sticky means nonvolatile
explanation: Sticky addresses are added to the running configuration only. Unsaved ones are lost at reload.

whyWrong.1: The MAC table is not a backup of configuration.
whyWrong.2: Learning does not make the address permanent.
whyWrong.3: Sticky does not save automatically.

prompt: R1 is the DHCP server on SW1 Gi0/1. SW1 Gi0/2 connects to SW2 Gi0/1, and clients are below SW2. Where do you set trust?
options: Trust only SW1 Gi0/2 because it is the inter-switch link
Leave both uplinks untrusted and trust only client ports
Trust both ports on SW1 and every client port on SW2
Trust SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1; leave SW1 Gi0/2 untrusted
explanation: Trust the ports where the real server's replies enter. Replies enter SW1 on Gi0/1 and SW2 on Gi0/1, and SW1's downlink Gi0/2 stays untrusted.

whyWrong.0: Server replies enter SW1 on Gi0/1, not Gi0/2.
whyWrong.1: Untrusted uplinks would drop the real server's replies.
whyWrong.2: Trusting client ports lets endpoints send server messages.

exhibit.title: R1 DHCP server diagnostics (summary)
exhibit.text:
Request received: giaddr 0.0.0.0, relay-agent information (Option 82) present
Request rejected by relay-information trust policy

prompt: The server-facing port is trusted, and the server rejects requests that carry Option 82 with giaddr 0.0.0.0. This lab does not need Option 82. What fixes it?
options: Make all client-facing interfaces trusted
Disable Option 82 insertion on the switch
Configure a new DHCP default gateway
Disable DHCP snooping on every VLAN
explanation: A snooping access switch inserts Option 82 by default, and the server rejects it. Enter no ip dhcp snooping information option on the switch.

whyWrong.0: Trusting client ports lets rogue servers answer.
whyWrong.2: A gateway setting does not stop the server rejecting requests.
whyWrong.3: Disabling snooping removes the protection.

prompt: A verified static printer has no snooping binding, so its ARP is dropped on an untrusted port. DHCP clients must keep using bindings. What do you do?
options: Add its MAC to the switch's ordinary forwarding table only
Permit its exact IP/MAC in an applied ARP ACL without `static`
Apply an ARP ACL with `static` and list only the printer
Exclude the printer from the DHCP allocation pool only
explanation: Permit the printer's exact IP and MAC in an ARP ACL and apply it without static. Without static, other hosts fall back to the snooping bindings.

whyWrong.0: A forwarding entry does not validate ARP.
whyWrong.2: With static, unlisted DHCP clients are denied with no fallback.
whyWrong.3: A DHCP exclusion does not authorize ARP.

prompt: The broadcast level crossed the rising threshold and now reads 0.7%. What does the displayed policy do?
options: All unicast traffic is discarded at the same threshold
Forwarding resumes whenever the rate falls below 1.00%
The port is necessarily error-disabled at 0.7%
Suppression continues until it falls below 0.50%
explanation: Once the rising threshold is crossed, broadcasts are dropped until the level falls below the falling threshold, which is 0.50%. At 0.7% suppression continues.

whyWrong.0: The policy affects broadcasts, not all unicast.
whyWrong.1: Traffic resumes only below the falling threshold, not the rising one.
whyWrong.2: The port is err-disabled only with storm-control action shutdown.

prompt: An RA guard host policy is defined, but unwanted RAs still enter an endpoint port. What is missing?
options: Clear the client’s old default route without changing ingress policy.
Redefine the same host policy without applying it to any port.
Attach the host policy to the actual endpoint ingress interface.
Attach a router-role policy to the endpoint to admit its advertisements.
explanation: A defined policy does nothing until you attach it. Enter ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy on the endpoint ingress port.

whyWrong.0: Clearing old state does not block new RAs.
whyWrong.1: Defining the policy again still does not apply it.
whyWrong.3: A router role would admit the advertisements.

prompt: You deploy RA guard on an access switch with one legitimate IPv6 router. Which two actions belong in the deployment? (Choose two.)
options: Judge success from the policy name alone
Assume DHCP snooping also validates IPv6 RAs
Attach the host policy to the endpoint ingress
Require old SLAAC addresses to disappear immediately
Confirm the legitimate router-facing role and fresh permitted RAs
explanation: Attach the host policy to endpoint ports and give the legitimate router's port the router role. Then check with fresh RAs, because hosts keep older addresses until lifetimes expire.

whyWrong.0: A policy name does not show it is applied.
whyWrong.1: DHCP snooping does not check IPv6 RAs.
whyWrong.3: Old addresses do not vanish immediately.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Secure maximum: 1; authorized secure MAC: A.
An isolated hub presents frames from A and new source B to this one port.
A’s traffic continues; B’s frames are dropped.
Port remains secure-up; violation counter increases and log records new violations.

prompt: Which violation mode matches the recorded behavior, where B is rejected and A keeps forwarding?
options: Shutdown: disable the entire port while keeping A’s frames forwarding.
Restrict: reject the additional source while reporting its violations.
Protect: reject the additional source while incrementing the same violation counters.
Disabled: admit both sources after the secure-address total is reached.
explanation: Restrict rejects the extra source and records violations while keeping the secure address forwarding. Protect does not report and shutdown stops the whole port.

whyWrong.0: Shutdown stops all traffic, A's included.
whyWrong.2: Protect does not count violations.
whyWrong.3: B was rejected, so enforcement is active.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
DAI enabled for VLAN 10; Fa0/2 is untrusted.
Snooping binding: 10.1.10.51, 00bb.0000.0002, VLAN 10, Fa0/2.
New ARP message: sender 10.1.10.51 / 00dd.0000.0009; ingress Fa0/2, VLAN 10.
No ARP ACL is configured.

prompt: Why does DAI drop the new ARP message?
options: The client uses a private IPv4 subnet rather than a public one.
The client’s IP address matches the binding’s IPv4 address.
The ARP sender claims a different MAC from the binding for that IP.
The switch has a client lease binding instead of a router binding.
explanation: The binding ties 10.1.10.51 to 00bb.0000.0002, but the ARP claims that IP with 00dd.0000.0009. The sender IP and MAC must both match a binding.

whyWrong.0: Private addressing is normal.
whyWrong.1: The IP matches, and the MAC is what differs.
whyWrong.3: A client lease binding is the right source for validation.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Applied ARP ACL for VLAN 10 has an explicit deny matching client 10.1.10.51 / 00bb.0000.0002.
The filter is applied without the static keyword.
A correct DHCP snooping binding also exists for the same client and ingress.
DAI is enabled; ingress untrusted.

prompt: What happens to the client's ARP under this policy?
options: The missing static keyword means all ARP ACL entries are ignored.
The explicit ACL deny rejects it even without the static keyword.
The correct binding overrides every configured ACL denial.
The ARP claim is accepted because its Ethernet source is unicast.
explanation: Without static, unmatched ARP falls back to the bindings, but an explicit deny entry still denies. The matching deny rejects the ARP.

whyWrong.0: Without static, ACL entries still apply.
whyWrong.2: A matching explicit deny is applied before any binding fallback.
whyWrong.3: A unicast source MAC does not bypass the policy.

prompt: A 1% broadcast threshold is copied from a 100 Mb/s port to a 1 Gb/s port. What rates result?
options: The faster port uses 100 Mb/s because the percentage is a packet count.
The thresholds correspond to about 1 Mb/s on the slower port and 10 Mb/s on the faster.
The slower port uses 10 Mb/s while the faster port uses 1 Mb/s.
Both ports use 1 Mb/s because the configured percentage is identical.
explanation: The threshold is a percentage of port bandwidth. 1% is 1 Mb/s at 100 Mb/s and 10 Mb/s at 1 Gb/s.

whyWrong.0: The percentage is not a packet count.
whyWrong.2: The values are swapped.
whyWrong.3: A percentage scales with bandwidth.

prompt: After RA guard is enforced, the client still lists an old IPv6 address and default router. What follows?
options: The policy must have stopped inspecting because the old address is still visible.
The presence of a default router proves its latest advertisement crossed this port.
DAI must erase all IPv6 addresses before RA guard can begin to work.
Old state can remain for its lifetime; inspect fresh RAs to judge current enforcement.
explanation: Learned addresses and routes stay until their lifetimes expire. Check fresh RAs to judge enforcement.

whyWrong.0: Old state alone does not show the policy failed.
whyWrong.1: The router entry may predate the policy.
whyWrong.2: DAI is an IPv4 ARP feature and does not reset IPv6 state.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Snooping is correctly enabled globally and for VLAN 10; server ingress trust is correct.
PC-A still uses a lease acquired earlier, before snooping was enabled.
R1 lists that lease; SW1’s binding table is empty.
The intended design will validate PC-A’s ARP through DAI.

prompt: Before DAI is enabled, which action supplies the missing binding?
options: Obtain a fresh DHCP exchange and verify the resulting switch binding.
Add the client’s MAC to the ordinary forwarding table without its IP.
Trust the client port so future ARP never needs a binding.
Save the switch configuration so it copies every client lease automatically.
explanation: The server lease came before snooping saw the exchange, so the switch has no binding. Get a fresh DHCP exchange and check the binding table.

whyWrong.1: A forwarding entry has no IP association.
whyWrong.2: Trusting the port bypasses inspection for the client.
whyWrong.3: Saving the configuration does not create bindings.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
PC-A MAC 00aa.0000.0001 is still explicitly secured on Fa0/1 in VLAN 10.
An approved move places PC-A on Fa0/2, also a secure VLAN 10 access port.
Fa0/2’s maximum is not full. The old secure entry was not removed.

prompt: A moved endpoint violates the second secure port, which has spare capacity. Why?
options: Port security requires the two ports to belong to different STP instances.
The ordinary MAC aging interval has not yet enabled additional secure capacity.
The same address remains secured on another interface in the same VLAN.
A secure source always consumes two entries whenever it sends an ARP request.
explanation: A violation also occurs when an address secured on one port appears on another secure port in the same VLAN. Remove the old secure entry from Fa0/1.

whyWrong.0: STP instances are not part of this rule.
whyWrong.1: MAC aging does not remove the secure entry.
whyWrong.3: ARP does not create a second secure entry.

exhibit.title: SW1 relevant configuration
exhibit.text:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 20
ip arp inspection vlan 10
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 ip arp inspection trust
!
DHCP snooping binding table: 0 entries

prompt: VLAN 10 clients have leases, but their ARP is dropped after DAI is enabled. Which fix supplies the missing bindings?
options: Enable snooping for VLAN 10, then obtain fresh client leases
Enable sticky MAC learning on every client-facing port
Add VLAN 20 to every client access port without changing IPs
Disable the clients' default gateways and renew their leases
explanation: DAI inspects VLAN 10, but snooping is configured only for VLAN 20, so no bindings exist. Enable snooping on VLAN 10 and get fresh leases.

whyWrong.1: Port-security entries are not DAI bindings.
whyWrong.2: Moving clients to VLAN 20 changes the design and does not fix VLAN 10.
whyWrong.3: A gateway setting does not create bindings.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved replacement MAC: 00bb.0000.0002.
Before power loss: running-config sticky entry 00bb.0000.0002; fresh traffic succeeds.
Startup-config sticky entry: 00aa.0000.0001.
No save occurred after replacement. Maximum 1; violation shutdown.

prompt: After a restart, why does the approved replacement endpoint fail the one-device policy?
options: The normal dynamic MAC-table aging timer immediately deletes every secure address.
The lower source MAC replaces any higher saved sticky address during root election.
A shutdown violation automatically writes the new endpoint into startup configuration.
The running replacement was never saved, so the old saved sticky address is restored.
explanation: The replacement was set up in running configuration only. At boot the switch loads the startup configuration, which still holds the old device's address.

whyWrong.0: Dynamic MAC aging does not delete secure addresses.
whyWrong.1: STP root election does not choose secure MACs.
whyWrong.2: A violation does not save the new endpoint.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Only R1, an approved static router/server, connects to SW1 Gi0/1.
Gi0/1: DHCP snooping trusted; DAI untrusted.
Client Fa0/1: fresh lease and correct snooping binding.
R1 10.1.10.1 has no DHCP-client binding or ARP ACL permit.
Capture: valid DHCP ACK reaches client; R1’s ARP reply enters Gi0/1 and DAI rejects it.
The approved design explicitly permits an ARP-inspection bypass only on R1’s controlled link.

prompt: DHCP trust works but the static router's ARP is rejected. Which narrow change fits this one-router design?
options: Raise the port-security maximum on the client because ARP uses an extra source.
Apply the separate intended DAI trust to the controlled router ingress.
Trust every client port for DHCP so the router can receive their requests.
Remove the client’s lease so DAI stops inspecting its gateway traffic.
explanation: DHCP trust admits server replies and does not authorize the router's ARP. Apply DAI trust to the router's ingress port.

whyWrong.0: No source-MAC limit violation is shown.
whyWrong.2: Trusting client ports for DHCP does not fix ARP.
whyWrong.3: Removing a valid binding does not authorize the router.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
VLAN 10 DAI enabled; client ports remain untrusted.
STATIC-HOSTS permits only verified printer 10.1.10.20 / 00cc.0000.0020.
ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10 static
All DHCP clients have correct fresh snooping bindings but no ACL permit.
Policy: permit printer’s exact pair and continue binding validation for DHCP clients.

prompt: The printer works, but DHCP clients fail ARP after the change. Which fix keeps the checks?
options: Add an ordinary static MAC forwarding entry for each affected DHCP client.
Remove only the static application keyword, retaining the printer permit and binding fallback.
Delete the printer permit because DHCP bindings automatically cover its excluded address.
Keep static and trust every client interface so none needs a binding check.
explanation: static makes the ACL's implicit deny final, so clients lose the binding fallback. Remove the static keyword and keep the printer permit.

whyWrong.0: Forwarding entries do not authorize ARP.
whyWrong.2: A DHCP exclusion creates no binding, so the printer needs its permit.
whyWrong.3: Trusting client ports bypasses inspection.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/6 DHCP rate limit: 15 packets/s; observed DHCP traffic below that rate.
Fa0/6 DAI allowance: 15 ARP packets/s, 1-second burst interval.
During a measured ARP burst, log names arp-inspection as the errdisable cause.
No MAC-security violation is recorded.

prompt: A port was err-disabled with an arp-inspection reason. Which policy do you check first?
options: The sticky MAC limit because every err-disabled port has exceeded it.
The STP root priority because the port is no longer forwarding.
The ARP inspection rate and actual ARP load on this interface.
The DHCP rate because its configured number also happens to be 15.
explanation: The log names arp-inspection, so the ARP rate limit was exceeded. Check the ARP inspection rate and the real ARP load.

whyWrong.0: No port-security violation is shown.
whyWrong.1: STP does not explain this errdisable cause.
whyWrong.3: DHCP traffic stayed below its limit.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Supported Catalyst RA guard implementation.
Gi1/0/24 is the only legitimate IPv6 router link.
Running configuration attaches ENDPOINTS, device-role host, on Gi1/0/24.
Fresh RA from fe80::1 is observed before switch ingress but not at the client.
The router sends correctly, VLAN path is verified, and IPv4 still works.
Design calls for a router-role policy on Gi1/0/24.

prompt: Which fix and check match the IPv6 evidence?
options: Remove the client’s IPv4 gateway because IPv4 reachability is interfering with router discovery.
Raise the DHCP snooping packet limit until the IPv6 router gains a binding.
Apply the intended router-role policy on the legitimate router ingress, then verify fresh authorized RAs.
Trust all endpoint ports as routers so every advertisement reaches the client.
explanation: The legitimate router's port was set to the host role. Attach the router-role policy there and verify fresh authorized RAs.

whyWrong.0: The IPv4 gateway is not the cause.
whyWrong.1: DHCPv4 snooping does not authorize RAs.
whyWrong.3: Making every endpoint a router defeats the policy.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text: Isolated supported-switch lab. R1 is the permitted router; R2 is the test router on a host-role ingress. Cables, VLAN and R2 configuration remain unchanged during the comparison.

prompt: Which two observations best show the RA policy works? (Choose two.)
options: The client retains an address learned before the test began.
The host-policy name appears in the saved configuration.
No R2 RA is seen during one short capture without first proving R2 transmits.
Legitimate R1 RAs continue reaching the client throughout the guarded comparison.
R2 RAs cross the same path when its host policy is removed, then cease after restoration over repeated observed intervals.
explanation: Legitimate R1 RAs keep arriving, and R2 RAs cross when its host policy is removed and stop when it is restored. The comparison proves R2 transmits and the policy blocks it.

whyWrong.0: Old learned state does not show current delivery.
whyWrong.1: A policy name does not prove it is attached.
whyWrong.2: A short silent capture could mean R2 sent nothing.

prompt: What is the default DHCP snooping trust state of a port?
options: Trusted
Untrusted
Trusted on trunks only
Trusted on uplinks only
explanation: Every port is untrusted by default. Trust only the ports where the real server's replies enter.

whyWrong.0: Ports are untrusted until you trust them.
whyWrong.2: Trust does not depend on port type.
whyWrong.3: Uplinks are untrusted too unless you configure trust.

prompt: What is the default ARP rate limit on an untrusted DAI port?
options: 1 packet per second
15 packets per second
100 packets per second
No limit
explanation: An untrusted DAI port is limited to 15 ARP packets per second. A trusted port has no limit.

whyWrong.0: 1 second is the burst interval, not the rate.
whyWrong.2: 100 packets per second is not the default.
whyWrong.3: Only trusted ports have no limit.

prompt: Which command enables automatic recovery of ports err-disabled by port security?
options: errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation
switchport port-security recovery
errdisable detect cause psecure
port-security auto-recover
explanation: errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation turns on timed recovery for port-security violations. The default interval is 300 seconds.

whyWrong.1: That is not the recovery command.
whyWrong.2: That is not the recovery command.
whyWrong.3: That is not the recovery command.

prompt: Which DHCP messages does snooping drop when they arrive on an untrusted port?
options: Discover and Request
Offer, ACK and NAK
Discover and Offer
Request and ACK
explanation: Server messages (Offer, ACK, NAK) are dropped on untrusted ports. Client messages (Discover, Request) are allowed.

whyWrong.0: Discover and Request are client messages and are allowed.
whyWrong.2: Discover is a client message, so it is not dropped.
whyWrong.3: Request is a client message, so it is not dropped.
